I am a huge movie buff, and have an extraordinary knowledge about Academy Award history. It is pretty ridiculous.

I am the type of person that has to watch movies in their original aspect ratio, watch commentaries and behind-the-scenes documentaries. Oftentimes, I will watch the same movie several times in a row because I tend to miss things on the first viewing as I am focused on other things. For instance, I may be concentrating on the framing / lighting / photography of the film during one watch, and then focusing on the story / dialogue / character development on another watch, and then keying into influences and references to other works. That kind of stuff. Because of this, it is typically better that I watch movies by myself.

When I was 14-years old-ish, I remember finding a World Almanac around our house, and it included a full list of Academy Award winning films in all of the major categories, and I had thought to myself, "well, if someone is saying these are the best, then maybe they are worth checking out." Which is exactly what I did. The public library became a weekly visit, and I would take home a batch of Oscar-winning films. The Academy and I have major disagreements on what should and should not have won, but I treat them as a fellow movie buff with differing opinions. It's fun to compare and contrast our views on films of merit. I ended up developing a reputation among people in my high school for knowing a ridiculous amount of information pertaining to classic films and the Academy Awards.

Fast forward to the Spring of 2010, and I attended an Oscar Party viewing at an art theater that I patron with my college girlfriend. Going in, I was really only expecting to watch the Oscars with a bunch of other movie geeks, and hoping that they might have a prediction pool (which any Oscar party worth attending has, but for some reason I've been to ones that didn't do them). When we walked in, the theater itself was doing a prediction pool, which made me happy. But then we heard that the bar that was adjacent to the theater was holding their own prediction pool, which made me even happier. I filled out both of them and hoped for the best. But then things got really interesting. I walked into the theater to watch the Oscars, and the theater manager who was hosting the event said they would be having an Oscar trivia contest during commercial breaks -- which I had no idea they were going to be doing. As soon as he mentioned this, I vividly remember thinking to myself, "Oh. My. God. I've been training for this for over a decade," and then turning to my college girlfriend saying, "I am going for blood." The way it was set up was that the first person to give a correct response would receive a prize (something like a T-shirt, or a poster, or a movie soundtrack, etc.), and for each one you got right, you were given a point, and the person with the most points at the end would get a grand-prize package. Right out of the gate, I was buzzing in for the gimme questions, the ridiculously easy ones. I actually started to feel bad, because the seats next to us were filling up with swag. People were rubber-necking me, and frustrated that I was being as aggressive as I was. So, I changed strategies. I wasn't going to buzz in anymore. I was going to let the question be asked, and if someone knew it and buzzed in, I would let them have it. I even became an ambassador to some of the people in the back that couldn't be heard by the host, but was able to confirm that their answer was correct -- "hey, the guys over here have the answer!" The reason I did this was because I was confident in my abilities. They were eventually going to get to the obscure questions. And, I was right. They did. I would wait for the question to be asked, hold off to see if anyone was going to buzz in, and if no one did, I would supply the correct answer and get the prize. No one had any excuse to be upset with me for knowing answers they didn't. It was no longer an issue of me being the quickest and beating people to the punch. It had come down to the fact that I had the most knowledge on the subject. Right through that last stretch, all that was happening was no one buzzing in, me providing the answer, collecting my prizes, and filling up two entire seats full of movie-related merchandise. By the end of the night, I was first place in points, and took home the grand-prize package, in addition to my two seats filled with swag. The theater manager even came up to me and told me how impressed he was that I had known so much about the Oscars -- and I didn't even have an opportunity to study-up beforehand! I walked in cold!

And if this wasn't enough, I got a phone call the next day. I had won the theater's prediction pool and the bar's prediction pool. In total, I received well over a thousand dollars in prizes. For years, I had this crazy obsession with reading about classic movies and the Academy Awards, and it had finally been justified, even if for only that night. They stopped doing the Oscar party after that year, and I like to think that it was because I completely slaughtered everyone and walked away as the undisputed champion and they feared that I would return again the following year -- which I would have, by the way, and I would have kicked everyone's ass again.

TLDR: I'm really into movies and the Academy Awards.
